title: The Theory of Advertising: A Simple Exposition of the Principles of Psychology in Their Relation to Successful Advertising
key_findings: (EBSCO research starter / catalogue records) One of the first books applying psychology to advertising; offers rules for attracting attention. Later editions retitled (Psychology of Advertising, 1908). Reviewed by E. L. Thorndike in 1904.
practical_applications: History: advertising psychology began as applied attention/suggestion psychology, long before modern evidence standards.
limitations: Content not read; edition/title confusion across scans.

title: Propaganda
key_findings: Chapter I 'Organizing Chaos' opens by calling 'the conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses' an important element in democratic society (quoted in search excerpts; text on Project Gutenberg #78634).
practical_applications: History/ethics: the founding text of PR openly frames persuasion as manipulation by an elite - the reason modern codes insist on transparency.
limitations: Only the opening passage seen via search; full text not read this session.

title: Confessions of an Advertising Man
key_findings: Published by Atheneum, 1963; >1,000,000 copies printed by 2008; widely assigned in advertising courses (secondary listings).
practical_applications: History: practitioner canon of research-led copy (headlines, facts, brand image).
limitations: Practitioner memoir, not evidence; the famous 'consumer isn't a moron' line could not be verified in the text this session.

title: Ad Age Advertising Century: Top 100 Advertising Campaigns
key_findings: Ranks Volkswagen 'Think Small' (Doyle Dane Bernbach, 1959) as no. 1 campaign of the 20th century (list dated 29 March 1999 per secondary sources).
practical_applications: Case: the 'creative revolution' (Bernbach) - honest, self-deprecating copy and art+copy teams.
limitations: Industry ranking by jury opinion, not an effectiveness measure; original adage.com page not retrieved (reprint only via search).

title: Broadening the Concept of Marketing
key_findings: Argues marketing is a pervasive societal activity beyond selling goods; asks whether marketing principles transfer to non-business organisations, persons and ideas.
practical_applications: History: why 'marketing' now covers clinics, causes, creators and personal brands - and why the same ethics apply.
limitations: Conceptual essay, no data.

title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
key_findings: Value assigned to gains and losses relative to a reference point; value function concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses; certainty and isolation effects; same choice in different forms gives inconsistent preferences.
practical_applications: Framing of offers (gain vs loss, reference price) - basis of behavioural-economics marketing.
limitations: Lab choices over money gambles; transfer to ad copy is indirect.

title: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017 - Press release
key_findings: Thaler awarded 'for his contributions to behavioural economics': limited rationality, social preferences, self-control; mental accounting; endowment effect; coined 'nudge'.
practical_applications: History: behavioural economics entered marketing practice mainly through Thaler/Kahneman popularisation.
limitations: Press release; prize is not evidence that every nudge works (see Maier2022).

title: The Elaboration Likelihood Model of Persuasion
authors: Petty, R. E.; Cacioppo, J. T.
key_findings: Original ELM statement (Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 19): central vs peripheral routes depending on motivation and ability to elaborate (bibliographic; >11,000 citations per OpenAlex).
practical_applications: Diagnose each piece: is the viewer able/motivated to think (high-involvement purchase) or scrolling (peripheral cues)?
limitations: Chapter not read this session; content stated only as commonly summarised by Kitchen2014.

title: Heuristic versus systematic information processing and the use of source versus message cues in persuasion
key_findings: High involvement: opinion change driven by number of arguments, not communicator likability; low involvement: driven by likable communicator, not arguments.
Content-mediated (systematic) opinion change persisted longer than source-mediated change.
practical_applications: Low-involvement scroll content: likable, credible source matters; consideration content (lens choice, price): real arguments matter and last longer.
limitations: Student samples, 1980 print messages.

title: The elaboration likelihood model: review, critique and research agenda
authors: Kitchen, P. J.; Kerr, G.; Schultz, D. E.; McColl, R.; Pals, H.
key_findings: Critiques ELM: descriptive nature, continuum questions (how people move between routes), multi-channel processing, mediating variables, need for replication; questions relevance to modern multi-media contexts.
Companion JAR replication (Kerr, Schultz & Kitchen) suggested planning frameworks built on ELM may not reflect digital consumers (search summary).
practical_applications: Use ELM as a diagnostic lens, not a predictive law; both routes can run at once.
limitations: Conceptual review.

title: The Role of Attitude toward the Ad as a Mediator of Advertising Effectiveness: A Test of Competing Explanations
authors: MacKenzie, S. B.; Lutz, R. J.; Belch, G. E.
key_findings: Structural-equation test of four models; dual mediation (A-ad affects brand attitude directly and via brand cognitions) fit best in a commercial pretest setting.
practical_applications: Liking the ad itself transfers to the brand - craft quality is not decoration.
limitations: Pretest setting; conditions specific.

title: Antecedents and Consequences of Attitude Toward the Ad: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Brown, S. P.; Stayman, D. M.
key_findings: Meta-analysis of A-ad relationships; significant between-study variance moderated by method variables; supports dual-mediation model with a larger indirect path (A-ad -> brand cognitions -> brand attitude).
practical_applications: Ad liking matters most when it makes people think better of the brand's attributes.
limitations: Mostly lab studies with forced exposure; 1992.

title: Measuring affective advertising: Implications of low attention processing on recall
key_findings: JAR 45(2):269-281. Proponent paper: argues claimed ad awareness (recall) underestimates the effect of emotional advertising compared with recognition-based measures (per search summary).
practical_applications: Recall-only metrics can undervalue emotional/brand pieces.
limitations: Abstract not retrieved; findings stated from search summary only.

title: High Attention Processing: The Real Power of Advertising
key_findings: Pre-test database: 97,083 respondents, 512 ads, 65 categories, US FMCG. Ads processed with high attention (recalled) had >2.5x the brand-choice impact of low-attention (recognised only) and ~6x ultra-low; new products: 9.8% vs 3.2% vs 1.4%.
States Heath's evidence was mainly case studies/anecdotes ('paucity of hard evidence').
practical_applications: Counter-evidence to over-reading 'low attention is enough'.
limitations: Commercial research firm with a stake in recall-based testing; not peer-reviewed; forced TV-program exposure.

title: The influence of ad-evoked feelings on brand evaluations: Empirical generalizations from consumer responses to more than 1000 TV commercials
authors: Pham, M. T.; Geuens, M.; De Pelsmacker, P.
key_findings: 1,576 Belgian consumers x 1,070 TV commercials, 150+ categories: ad-evoked feelings substantially affect brand evaluations, directly and via attitude toward the ad; not dependent on category involvement; somewhat stronger for hedonic than utilitarian products.
practical_applications: Feelings matter even for 'rational' categories like optical; a bit more for fashion frames/sunglasses than for lens tech.
limitations: Read via search summaries of abstract (author PDF exists, not opened); TV, Belgium.

title: Double Jeopardy Revisited
authors: Ehrenberg, A. S. C.; Goodhardt, G. J.; Barwise, T. P.
key_findings: Small brands have far fewer buyers and those buyers buy slightly less often ('double jeopardy'); reviews wide empirical evidence, theories, exceptions and implications.
practical_applications: Growth for a small shop mostly means more buyers (reach/penetration), not squeezing loyalty from a few.
limitations: Repeat-purchase categories; eyewear is infrequent purchase - pattern plausible but untested for it.

title: Conceptualizing and measuring brand salience
key_findings: Brand salience = the brand's propensity to be noticed or come to mind in buying situations; reflects quantity and quality of memory structures; broader than top-of-mind awareness.
practical_applications: Plan content around buying situations (category entry points), not just 'awareness'.
limitations: Conceptual; measurement proposed, not validated here.

title: How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know
key_findings: (Bibliographic + review summaries) Brands grow mainly via penetration; double jeopardy; mental and physical availability; distinctiveness over perceived differentiation. Reviewers note partial use of evidence and that it does not study how brands become established.
practical_applications: Reach broadly, be easy to notice/recognise/buy; keep distinctive assets constant.
limitations: Book not read; critiques came from reviews (search summary).

title: Answering critics
key_findings: Rebuts critiques: growth is mainly penetration but bigger brands also have slightly higher loyalty (the 'double' in DJ); cites longitudinal work (McDonald & Ehrenberg 2003; Graham 2012; JBR 2014); says attitude-predicts-behaviour findings reflect regression to the mean; asks critics to publish data.
practical_applications: Use the laws as base rates; treat 'loyalty is dead' as a misreading.
limitations: Self-defence by the school's director; undated (~10 years old).

title: The Long and the Short of It: Balancing Short and Long-Term Marketing Strategies (and follow-ups, as described by IPA)
authors: Binet, L.; Field, P. (IPA); blog by Hoad, A.
key_findings: IPA (2013) report found ~60:40 brand-building:activation budget sweet spot; Effectiveness in Context (2018) 62:38; as short-term campaigns rose, very large business effects in IPA cases fell; cited in 70+ academic works (IPA blog, 13 Sep 2023).
practical_applications: Keep a standing brand-building line (story carousels, brand clips) beside promos.
limitations: Report itself not read; ratio is an average across categories (Field), not a rule; data pre-COVID.

title: Les Binet and Peter Field: The Long and the Short of It (summary)
key_findings: Summary: 996 IPA-entered campaigns 1980-2010; emotional campaigns ~2x as likely to give top-box profit growth long-term; recruitment beats loyalty campaigns; share of voice above market share predicts growth; fame campaigns strongest.
practical_applications: Emotional/fame-oriented brand work for long-term; activation for now.
limitations: Blog summary with an internal contradiction; no methods; correlational IPA data.

title: Good, better, best and f*** the rest? (IPA blog, Binet response to Harry Guild's critique)
key_findings: Critic (Guild, BBH) argues IPA databank is a biased sample of award entries and correlations mislead; Binet concedes sample 'still somewhat biased' even including rejected cases, defends variation as sufficient.
practical_applications: Treat IPA findings as strong practitioner evidence, not causal proof.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Creativity in Advertising: When It Works and When It Doesn't
key_findings: HBR June 2013 (page metadata read). Per secondary summaries: 437 German TV campaigns for 90 FMCG brands (2005-2010) rated on five creativity dimensions (originality, flexibility, elaboration, synthesis, artistic value) and linked to sales; elaboration had a stronger sales effect than originality; creativity paid most in low-creativity categories.
practical_applications: Elaboration = rich, detailed execution of one idea: detail punch-ins, material close-ups, worked-out scenes.
limitations: Body text paywalled; numbers from student slides/summaries only - do not quote figures; FMCG Germany.

title: A Meta-Analysis of When and How Advertising Creativity Works
authors: Rosengren, S.; Eisend, M.; Koslow, S.; Dahlen, M.
key_findings: 93 data sets, 67 papers, 878 effect sizes: robust positive effects of ad creativity; both originality and appropriateness matter; stronger for high-involvement products; affect transfer, processing and signalling jointly explain effects (originality -> affect transfer, appropriateness -> signalling); calls for sales and digital research.
practical_applications: Novel AND on-brief; for considered purchases (lenses, premium frames) creativity pays more.
limitations: Mostly ad/brand reactions, few sales outcomes; little digital-video data.
license: CC BY / open access (per OpenAlex OA link)

title: Social Influence: Compliance and Conformity
authors: Cialdini, R. B.; Goldstein, N. J.
key_findings: Reviews 1997-2002 compliance/conformity research: susceptibility driven by goals of accuracy, affiliation and positive self-concept; influence often subtle and outside awareness.
practical_applications: Principles (social proof, reciprocity, commitment, authority, liking, scarcity) work through these goals - use them truthfully.
limitations: Review of mostly Western lab/field work.

title: A Room with a Viewpoint: Using Social Norms to Motivate Environmental Conservation in Hotels
authors: Goldstein, N. J.; Cialdini, R. B.; Griskevicius, V.
key_findings: Two hotel field experiments: descriptive-norm signs beat standard environmental appeal; 'provincial' norms (guests in this room) most effective.
practical_applications: Truthful, local social proof ('many Hua Hin customers choose...') is a candidate - if true and countable.
limitations: See BohnerSchluter2014 for failed replication.

title: A Room with a Viewpoint Revisited: Descriptive Norms and Hotel Guests' Towel Reuse Behavior
key_findings: Two German hotels (N=724; N=204): both standard and norm messages raised reuse vs no message, but descriptive-norm messages were NOT more effective than the standard message; proximity effects inconsistent.
practical_applications: Social proof is not a guaranteed upgrade; test it.
limitations: Cultural context differs (Germany); high baseline reuse.

title: Scarcity tactics in marketing: A meta-analysis of product scarcity effects on consumer purchase intentions
authors: Barton, B.; Zlatevska, N.; Oppewal, H.
key_findings: 416 effect sizes, 131 studies: scarcity cues generally raise purchase intentions; demand-based scarcity best for utilitarian products, supply-based for experiences, time-based for high-involvement products.
practical_applications: Real limits (genuine end date, real stock) can be stated; type of scarcity should fit product.
limitations: Purchase intention, not behaviour; does not address deception/trust costs.

title: The downside of scarcity: Scarcity appeals can trigger consumer anger and brand switching intentions
authors: Biraglia, A.; Usrey, B.; Ulqinaku, A.
key_findings: Two studies (experimental + correlational): consumers who fail to get a product advertised with limited-quantity appeals show higher intention to switch to competitors, mediated by anger.
practical_applications: If you announce 'limited', make sure people who miss out get an alternative (waitlist, similar frame).
limitations: Psychology & Marketing; two studies; intentions.

title: Consumers Are Becoming Wise to Your Nudge
key_findings: Survey-experiment, 2,102 UK adults shown nine real hotel-booking scarcity/social-proof claims: 65% saw them as sales pressure, 49% likely to distrust the company, 34% negative emotion, only 16% believed the claims.
practical_applications: Fake-feeling urgency costs trust.
limitations: Consultancy study, not peer-reviewed; hypothetical booking; self-report.

title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
authors: Mathur, A.; Acar, G.; Friedman, M. J.; Lucherini, E.; Mayer, J.; Chetty, M.; Narayanan, A.
key_findings: ~53K product pages, ~11K sites: 1,818 dark-pattern instances, 15 types in 7 categories (incl. urgency, scarcity, social proof); 183 sites deceptive; 22 third parties sell dark patterns as turnkey.
practical_applications: Countdown timers, fake stock and fake 'X people viewing' are documented deceptive patterns - never use.
limitations: Web shops; detection automated.

title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report)
key_findings: Sept 2022 staff report: 'design elements that induce false beliefs' include countdown timers on offers that are not time-limited, false sold-out claims, false claims that others are viewing/buying.
practical_applications: Regulator view: false urgency/scarcity is deception, not 'growth hacking'.
limitations: Read only via law-firm summaries this session; US jurisdiction (Thai law: see ETHICS file).

title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
authors: Scheibehenne, B.; Greifeneder, R.; Todd, P. M.
key_findings: 63 conditions, 50 experiments, N=5,036: mean choice-overload effect virtually zero with considerable variance; no sufficient conditions identified.
practical_applications: Do not assume 'fewer options always sells more'.
limitations: Later meta (Chernev2015) finds moderated effects.

title: Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis
authors: Chernev, A.; Boeckenholt, U.; Goodman, J. K.
key_findings: 99 observations, N=7,202: overload depends on choice-set complexity, task difficulty, preference uncertainty and effort-minimising goal; with moderators the effect is significant.
practical_applications: Overload is likely when customers lack preferences and options are hard to compare (e.g. lens coatings) - curate 2-3 and explain.
limitations: Mostly lab tasks.

title: When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing?
authors: Iyengar, S. S.; Lepper, M. R.
key_findings: Three studies: more people bought jam/chocolate or did essays when offered 6 vs 24-30 options; higher satisfaction with limited sets.
practical_applications: Origin of the 'jam study' - cite with Scheibehenne2010 null meta.
limitations: Classic single studies; replication mixed.

title: Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis
authors: Huber, J.; Payne, J. W.; Puto, C.
key_findings: Adding an option dominated by one item but not another can increase choice of the dominating item (decoy/attraction effect).
practical_applications: Origin of decoy pricing.
limitations: Stylised numeric attributes; see Frederick2014, Trendl2021.

title: The Limits of Attraction
authors: Frederick, S.; Lee, L.; Baskin, E.
key_findings: Attraction effect may be restricted to stylised numeric product descriptions; typically absent when products are experienced or when even one attribute is shown perceptually (e.g. photo); questions practical significance.
practical_applications: Decoys on visual product posts (frames shown as photos) are unlikely to work - and look manipulative.
limitations: Disputed by Huber et al. 2014 (not read).

title: A zero attraction effect in naturalistic choice
authors: Trendl, A.; Stewart, N.; Mullett, T. L.
key_findings: First experiment meeting Huber et al.'s (2014) criteria for naturalistic tests found a precisely zero attraction effect.
practical_applications: Same: do not build promos on decoy tricks.
limitations: One experiment; Decision journal.

title: No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
authors: Maier, M.; Bartos, F.; Stanley, T. D.; Shanks, D. R.; Harris, A. J. L.; Wagenmakers, E.-J.
key_findings: PNAS letter re-analysing Mertens et al. (2022) nudge meta-analysis with robust Bayesian meta-analysis: after adjusting for publication bias, no evidence remains for nudging overall; authors later said 'no overall evidence' (heterogeneity, some domains may work).
practical_applications: Behavioural 'hacks' have small, variable effects - test, don't assume.
limitations: Read via search summaries (PNAS blocked); letter, debated by Mertens et al.

title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories
authors: Tannenbaum, M. B.; Hepler, J.; Zimmerman, R. S.; Saul, L.; Jacobs, S.; Wilson, K.; Albarracin, D.
key_findings: 127 articles, 248 samples, N=27,372: fear appeals positively affect attitudes, intentions, behaviours (random-effects d=0.29); stronger with efficacy statements, high depicted susceptibility and severity, one-time behaviours, more female audiences; very few backfire circumstances.
practical_applications: UV/pterygium or presbyopia messages: show risk honestly + an easy one-time action (eye test, UV lens).
limitations: Mostly health domains; d is small-to-moderate.

title: The Influence of Source Credibility on Communication Effectiveness
key_findings: Subjects discounted material from untrustworthy sources at exposure, but over time dissociated content from source and scepticism faded (sleeper effect).
practical_applications: Credibility of the speaker matters at exposure; long-term, the message content travels on its own - so the content must be true.
limitations: 1951; sleeper effect later found fragile.

title: The Persuasiveness of Source Credibility: A Critical Review of Five Decades' Evidence
key_findings: Main-effect studies show high-credibility sources beat low; interaction studies show credibility can be a liability under some conditions; moderators: source, message, channel, receiver, destination variables.
practical_applications: Use the real optometrist/staff as source for health facts; credibility is conditional, not magic.
limitations: Narrative review.

title: The Persuasion Knowledge Model: How People Cope with Persuasion Attempts
key_findings: People develop knowledge about persuasion agents' goals and tactics and use it to cope; this shapes attitudes toward products and marketers.
practical_applications: When a tactic is recognised (fake urgency, hidden ad), it changes how the whole brand is judged.
limitations: Conceptual model.

title: 'This Post is Sponsored': Effects of Sponsorship Disclosure on Persuasion Knowledge and Electronic Word of Mouth in the Context of Facebook
authors: Boerman, S. C.; Willemsen, L. M.; Van Der Aa, E. P.
key_findings: 2x2 experiment: 'Sponsored' disclosure activated persuasion knowledge only when a celebrity (not the brand) posted; recognition of advertising -> distrusting beliefs -> lower eWOM intention.
practical_applications: Own-brand posts are already understood as ads; partner/creator posts must disclose.
limitations: Single Dutch experiment.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Disclosing Sponsored Content
authors: Eisend, M.; van Reijmersdal, E. A.; Boerman, S. C.; Tarrahi, F.
key_findings: 61 papers, 57 data sets: disclosure lowers brand attitudes, credibility and source evaluation but raises recognition, persuasion knowledge, resistance - and memory; content, timing, awareness moderate effects.
practical_applications: Disclosure costs a little persuasion but is legally/ethically required; it can even aid memory.
limitations: Mostly Western experiments.

title: Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising (16 CFR Part 255, revised)
key_findings: Revised 26 July 2023: material connections must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously (defined); platform built-in tools may be inadequate; disclosure behind 'more' is not unavoidable; virtual influencers count as endorsers; advertisers expected to monitor influencers.
practical_applications: International benchmark for creator/partner posts and AI characters.
limitations: US rules; read via law-firm summaries; Thai rules in ETHICS file.

title: Moment-to-Moment Optimal Branding in TV Commercials: Preventing Avoidance by Pulsing
authors: Teixeira, T. S.; Wedel, M.; Pieters, R.
key_findings: Eye tracking on 31 commercials, ~2,000 participants, zapping data: attention dispersion predicts avoidance; central on-screen brand positions (not brand size) promote avoidance; brand 'pulsing' (short repeated brand appearances, same total exposure) significantly reduced avoidance (simulation + controlled experiment).
practical_applications: Brand early AND repeatedly in short pulses, small and integrated - not one big centred logo slab.
limitations: TV ads, 2010; zapping in lab.

title: Decoding Digital Video Environments
authors: Meta + Realeyes (with eye square, Bill Harvey Consulting)
key_findings: Meta-commissioned lab study, 16,835 ad impressions from 6,076 US mobile users (Dec 2022), simulated Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Hulu, Snapchat, Twitter.
Feed and short-form show an intense initial burst of attention; ads with the strongest creative branding in those seconds scored highest in brand recognition; recommends a 'first second strategy'.
Brand recognition similar across environments; feed/short form ~0.16-0.17 brand recallers per attentive second vs stream ~0.07; causal impact of attention on recall cannot be measured in this design.
practical_applications: Put product + brand cue in the first 1-2 s of Reels/TikTok; do not save the logo for the end.
limitations: Platform-commissioned; US; lab simulation; correlational on attention.

title: What actually makes short-form video ads work? (Meta x Toluna study)
key_findings: ~100 ads x 100 viewers each in DE, UK, IT, TR; 65+ creative variables; top 20% vs average: brand + core message in first 5 s -> 1.7x more likely strong purchase intent; branding repeated through the ad (vs end logo only) 1.8x; audio+visual beats visual only; native/lower-fidelity, direct-to-camera performed well; for conversion ads, branding under ~25% of duration better.
practical_applications: Recurrent, integrated branding; native style; sound on.
limitations: Blog post (4 Aug 2026) summarising commissioned study; small ad sample; purchase intent; 'probability drivers, not rules'.

title: About the ABCDs of effective video ads (Google Ads Help)
key_findings: Attention, Branding, Connection, Direction. Branding: 'show up early and throughout'; audio brand mentions improve onscreen brand visuals. Claims up to 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and 17% in long-term brand contribution (Google/Kantar, April 2021).
practical_applications: Brand early + throughout + say the name in VO.
limitations: Platform guidance; methods of the Kantar study not described.

title: A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook
authors: Gordon, B. R.; Zettelmeyer, F.; Bhargava, N.; Chapsky, D.
key_findings: Observational methods often fail to recover the treatment effects measured by randomised advertising experiments on Facebook.
practical_applications: Only a randomised holdout (lift test) shows incrementality; platform attribution is not proof.
limitations: Large advertisers; abstract only.

title: The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising
authors: Lewis, R. A.; Rao, J. M.
key_findings: 25 field experiments ($2.8M spend): median ROI confidence interval >100 percentage points wide; sales very volatile relative to ad cost; informative experiments may need >10 million person-weeks; selection bias cripples observational methods.
practical_applications: A small shop cannot measure sales ROI of one ad precisely - use leading indicators + long-run tracking, be humble.
limitations: US retailers/brokerages.

title: Survey shows most optical products purchased in store (Vision Council Focused inSights 2024)
key_findings: 121,288 US adults (Jan 2022-Dec 2023): 85% of prescription eyeglasses, 79% of non-Rx readers, 77% of non-Rx sunglasses bought in person; 37% of contact lenses acquired online; no data on 'why'.
practical_applications: Eyewear is still a physical-store purchase: content's job is to bring people to the shop (physical availability).
limitations: US; news report of industry survey.

title: New Report Examines Consumers' Eyewear Purchasing Decisions (Jobson 2013 Eyewear & Eyecare Consumer Patterns)
key_findings: US Rx wearers (VisionWatch, March 2013): 66% bought eyeglasses where they had the exam; 72% chose frames in under an hour; 55% said the dispenser was very/somewhat important in the final decision; 83% rated dispenser help excellent/good.
practical_applications: Staff advice and the exam are the decisive touchpoints - show the people and the fitting process.
limitations: US, 2013, insurance-driven market unlike Thailand.

title: Specsavers: I Don't Go (IPA Effectiveness Awards Gold)
key_findings: Campaign played off the long-running 'Should've gone to Specsavers' line by addressing rejecters ('I don't go to Specsavers'); Home Visits volumes +32%; ~582,000 previous rejecters booked an eye test; est. GBP 19.8m incremental profit.
practical_applications: Consistent distinctive line for decades, then a twist that targets non-buyers.
limitations: Award entry written by agency/client; method not shown on page.

title: Should've gone to Specsavers: A far-sighted view of advertising's role in building a business over 30 years (IPA 2014 Gold)
authors: Philip, M. (Manning Gottlieb OMD) for Specsavers
key_findings: IPA Effectiveness Gold 2014: how Specsavers grew from 1984 launch to the largest UK optical market share via long-term advertising (search summary).
practical_applications: Long-term humour-based brand line in optical retail.
limitations: Paywalled; only listing seen.

title: After Uproar, Pepsi Halts Rollout Of Controversial Protest-Themed Ad
key_findings: Pepsi pulled its Kendall Jenner protest-themed ad on 5 April 2017, about a day after release: 'Clearly we missed the mark, and we apologize'; criticised for trivialising social-justice protests.
practical_applications: Failure case: borrowing a serious cause without earning it.
limitations: News reports via search; sales impact not documented.
